Car Nut Bought Split-Bumper 1972 Camaro Sight Unseen, Who Can Tell if It's a Real RS, or a Tribute
46 photos
Photo: YouTube/Show Me Your Car
Chevrolet executives nearly slipped on a giant banana peel in 1972 and axed the Camaro moniker altogether, turning Detroit into a slapstick comedy of corporate panic. A grueling 174-day strike at Norwood jammed the assembly line like a cream pie in the face, while incoming 1973 bumper rules forced the scrapping of 1,100 unfinished cars. Brass panicked over low output before cooler heads saved the badge from becoming a punchline.
The Camaro went on the rollercoaster of its life in the seventies, from the abyss of the early years to the peak of 1979, the greatest moment of the moniker (in sales, anyway). One of those ‘72s recently caught the eye of Craig Glenn, the roaming YouTuber from the Show Me Your Car channel. The car belongs to Mike Darty, who bought it back in May sight unseen as a birthday present to himself from Streetside Classics in Atlanta, Georgia, and just got it back on the road.
According to the Streetside Classics listing , the car is a 1972 Chevrolet Camaro RS tribute, and the asking price was $30,995 with 68,060 miles shown, and a 350 V8 paired with a 3-speed automatic transmission. The listing highlighted Mohave Gold paint, a crisp white vinyl top, Covert interior trim, 15-inch rally wheels with 235/60R15 tires, a 10-bolt rear axle, and a numbers-matching 350 engine.
Under the hood, the spec sheet notes a numbers-matching 350 cubic-inch V8 painted Chevy Orange with a FiTech fuel injection system, controller in the glove box, Edelbrock Performer EPS intake, polished Chevrolet valve covers, and long tube headers feeding dual exhaust with Borla mufflers. Power steering, air conditioning, front power disc and rear power drum brakes, and a RetroSound radio round out the build.
Photo: YouTube/Show Me Your Car Mike adds his own garage-floor slapstick to the story, having fitted fresh front suspension components, new brakes, and black wheels with fresh tires after the dry-rotted rubber nearly gave up the ghost. He also washed the car after towing it back from Lebanon so the white vinyl top would dry on the drive home, keeping a clean cabin with working lights, covert custom cloth, and a 130-mph speedometer.
Across its full run, the Camaro moniker spans production years 1966 to 2002 and 2009 to 2023 across six generations, with model years running from 1967 through 2002 and 2010 through 2024. The second generation from 1970 through 1981 holds the longest production run at 12 model years, surviving fuel scares, shifting regulations, and plenty of Detroit boardroom pratfalls.
In total volume, the second generation leads the entire Camaro family with 1,959,879 units built over its 12 model years, outpacing every other era by sheer cumulative weight. By contrast, the first generation from 1967 through 1969 takes the highest yearly average at roughly 233,046 cars per model year across 699,138 total builds, proving how quickly the pony car caught fire out of the gate.
Photo: YouTube/Show Me Your Car For the sake of historic accuracy, we should point out that the 1969 production year was extended through November 1969, instead of ending in July as traditionally. The cause of delay was tooling issues, forcing the execs to prolong the first generation by a few extra months. That’s the reason for a 243k- pony car production record scored that season.
For 1972, total Camaro production landed at 68,651 cars in standard reference tallies, as labor disputes tripped up Chevrolet at every turn. Out the 365 days between one production year to the next, the 1972 season was marred by 174 strike days. Buyers fortunate enough to get one could order the base Sport Coupe, the Z22 Rally Sport package, the Z27 Super Sport package, or the Z28 Special Performance Package. Convertibles were off the books in the second generation, leaving coupes to carry the show.
Powertrains for 1972 debuted SAE net horsepower ratings, starting with the 250-cubic-inch inline-six rated at 110 horsepower and the 307 V8 rated at 130 horsepower. Small-block 350 V8 choices included the two-barrel L65 at 165 horsepower and four-barrel L48 at 200 horsepower, while the Z28-exclusive solid-lifter LT-1 350 made 255 horsepower and the big-block 396/402 LS3 delivered 240 horsepower.
Photo: YouTube/Show Me Your Car What set the 1972 RS apart from regular Camaros was its split front bumperette arrangement and body-colored grille surround with round auxiliary and parking lights tucked beside the headlights. Non-RS models used a full front bumper and lower square parking lights instead. Meanwhile, Z28 and SS focused on powertrain hardware, whereas RS was a trim package available on base, SS, or Z28 cars.
Compared with first-generation RS models, the second-generation RS dropped hideaway headlights completely—a slapstick relief for anyone tired of vacuum doors sticking like stubborn dresser drawers. It also traded full front bumpers for split bumperettes and replaced dual headlights per side with single round lamps rather than a quad headlight layout, giving the early second-gen RS its unmistakable gaping fish mouth face.
Production numbers for 1972 break down into 4,821 six-cylinder Sport Coupes and 63,830 V8 Sport Coupes, spread between 11,364 Rally Sports, 6,562 SSs, and 2,575 Z28s. 27,009 cars received the L65 350 two-barrel V8 and 970 Super Sports received the LS3 396/402 big-block V8.
Photo: YouTube/Show Me Your Car Transmission choices for 1972 include 4,127 M20 wide-ratio 4-speeds, 942 M21 close-ratio 4-speeds, and 767 M22 heavy-duty close-ratio 4-speeds, plus 4,462 Powerglide 2-speed automatics and 7,302 Turbo Hydra-Matic 3-speed automatics alongside standard 3-speed manuals.
Base price for the cheapest 1972 Camaro—the six-cylinder Sport Coupe—was $2,729.70, while the V8 coupe started at $2,819.70. The RS package cost $118. Rounding out the 1972 order sheet, RPO Z27 (Super Sport) cost $306.35, while the Z28 was $769.15.
